draft.title: Activity networks
card: A big project is split into smaller jobs called activities. An activity network shows them as a diagram.
Each activity is an edge (an arrow) with a letter and its duration, such as A, 3 for an activity A that takes 3 hours. Each arrow points in the direction of time.
Some activities must wait for others. A vertex (a circle) is where arrows meet, and any activity leaving a vertex cannot start until every activity arriving at it is finished.
Example: A, 2 leads to a vertex. Two arrows leave it: B, 4 and C, 3. B and C can only start once A is done. B and C do not wait for each other.
draft.remember: In an activity network, edges are activities with durations, and an activity waits for all arrows into its starting vertex.

a.q: In an activity network, activities D and E both arrive at a vertex, and activity F leaves it. When can F start?
opts: Once both D and E are finished
As soon as D is finished
As soon as E is finished
At the same time as D and E
a.why: F leaves the vertex, so it must wait for every activity arriving there. That means both D and E must be finished. Starting after only one of them is tempting, but F would then begin before the other is done.
a.clue: An activity waits for everything arriving at its starting vertex.

b.q: Mia plans a school fair. Activity P, 3 days (book the hall) leads to a vertex. Activities Q, 2 days (print posters) and R, 4 days (hire tables) both leave that vertex. Which statement is correct?
opts: Q and R can both start once P is finished
Q can start only after R is finished
R can start before P is finished
P can start only after Q and R are finished
b.why: Q and R both leave the vertex where P arrives, so each must wait for P and no other activity. They do not wait for each other. P is before them, so it cannot wait for Q or R.
b.clue: Look at which arrows enter the vertex and which leave it.

a.best: Once both D and E are finished

b.best: Q and R can both start once P is finished
